```text
domain:
    i: dim in [0, N)
    j: dim in [0, N)

data:
    # Matrix A as in PolyBench C: A[i][j], row-major
    A[i, j]: in DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j

    # Vectors
    x1[i]: inout DATA_TYPE = i -> i          # updated in first mat-vec
    x2[i]: inout DATA_TYPE = i -> i          # updated in second mat-vec
    y1[i]: in DATA_TYPE = i -> i
    y2[i]: in DATA_TYPE = i -> i

parameters:
    # Tunable constants for cache and SIMD on the target machine
    T_I: int  # tile size for i-dimension (e.g., 64 or 128)
    T_J: int  # tile size for j-dimension (e.g., 64 or 128)
    V:   int  # SIMD width (e.g., 8 for AVX2 float, 4 for AVX2 double)

computation:
    # Initialization (matches init_array; included for completeness)
    INIT_X1:
        for i:
            x1[i] = (DATA_TYPE)((i          % N) / (DATA_TYPE)N)
    INIT_X2:
        for i:
            x2[i] = (DATA_TYPE)(((i + 1)    % N) / (DATA_TYPE)N)
    INIT_Y1:
        for i:
            y1[i] = (DATA_TYPE)(((i + 3)    % N) / (DATA_TYPE)N)
    INIT_Y2:
        for i:
            y2[i] = (DATA_TYPE)(((i + 4)    % N) / (DATA_TYPE)N)
    INIT_A:
        for i, j:
            A[i, j] = (DATA_TYPE)(((i * j)  % N) / (DATA_TYPE)N)

    # Kernel mvt, mathematical form:
    #
    #   x1[i] = x1[i] + sum_j A[i, j] * y1[j]
    #   x2[i] = x2[i] + sum_j A[j, i] * y2[j]
    #
    # We keep this as the reference semantics; all loop transforms
    # below are legality-preserving rearrangements of these sums.

    K1:  # x1 = x1 + A * y1
        for i:
            x1[i] = x1[i] + sum(j, A[i, j] * y1[j])

    K2:  # x2 = x2 + A^T * y2
        for i:
            x2[i] = x2[i] + sum(j, A[j, i] * y2[j])

dependencies:
    # Initialization must complete before using the data
    for i in [0, N):
        INIT_A(i, *)   -> K1
        INIT_A(i, *)   -> K2
        INIT_X1(i)     -> K1
        INIT_X2(i)     -> K2
        INIT_Y1(i)     -> K1
        INIT_Y2(i)     -> K2

optimization:
    #------------------------------
    # 1) Optimize K1: x1 = x1 + A * y1
    #------------------------------

    # Block i to create coarse-grain tasks and improve cache reuse of y1 and rows of A.
    # I1 is the outer tile index, i1 the intra-tile index (re-uses the original name i).
    block(K1.i, I1, T_I)          # for K1: i -> (I1, i)

    # Block j (reduction dimension) to improve cache locality for A and y1.
    # This induces partial sums over j-tiles that are accumulated into x1[i].
    # (Legal because + is associative/commutative for DATA_TYPE.)
    block(K1.j, J1, T_J)          # for K1 reduction: j -> (J1, j)

    # Parallelize across tiles of i; each tile writes a disjoint slice of x1[*].
    parallelize(I1)

    # Vectorize across j within each tile: A[i, j] and y1[j] are both contiguous
    # in row-major layout, so this generates wide SIMD loads and FMAs.
    vectorize(K1.j, V)

    # Optionally unroll the small inner i-loop within a tile to reduce loop overhead
    # and allow scalar x1[i] to stay in registers longer.
    unroll(K1.i, 4)

    #------------------------------
    # 2) Optimize K2: x2 = x2 + A^T * y2
    #------------------------------

    # Semantically we keep:
    #   x2[i] = x2[i] + sum_j A[j, i] * y2[j]
    # but we want to traverse A row-major. We achieve this via:
    #  - strip-mining i
    #  - interchanging the inner i (within a tile) with j
    # so that the innermost loop runs over contiguous columns of a fixed row j.
    #
    # This yields an execution order equivalent to:
    #
    #   for I2 in tiles of i:                          # parallel dimension
    #     for j in [0, N):                             # reduction over rows
    #       t = y2[j]
    #       for i in tile I2:                          # independent updates
    #         x2[i] += A[j, i] * t
    #
    # which has:
    #   - good locality on A[j, *] and x2[*]
    #   - parallelism across tiles I2
    #   - increased reuse of y2[j].

    block(K2.i, I2, T_I)          # i -> (I2, i) for K2

    # Interchange the inner i within a tile with the reduction index j.
    # After this, loops are ordered as: I2 (outer), j (middle), i (inner).
    interchange(K2.j, K2.i)

    # Parallelize across i-tiles; each tile updates a disjoint slice x2[i].
    parallelize(I2)

    # Vectorize across i within each tile; A[j, i] and x2[i] are contiguous
    # in row-major storage when j is fixed.
    vectorize(K2.i, V)

    # Optionally block j for better reuse of x2[i] and y2[j] in cache.
    block(K2.j, J2, T_J)

    #------------------------------
    # 3) General notes on memory and temporaries
    #------------------------------

    # - No global data layout change: A remains a single row-major N×N array.
    # - We do not materialize a full transpose of A (which would double memory).
    #   Instead, the K2 schedule only uses a strip-mined, reordered traversal.
    # - Extra storage is limited to:
    #     * scalar temporaries per thread (e.g., t = y2[j])
    #     * loop-index bookkeeping
    #   which is far below the 50% overhead limit relative to A, x1, x2, y1, y2.
```

```text
domain:
    i: dim in [0, N)          # row index
    j: dim in [0, N)          # column index

data:
    # Matrix A and vectors as in the original C code:
    #   x1[i]  = x1[i] + sum_j A[i][j] * y1[j]
    #   x2[i]  = x2[i] + sum_j A[j][i] * y2[j]
    #
    # Use a row-major layout for A to make the j-loop (column index) the
    # fastest-varying dimension, which matches the inner loop in the first
    # MV product and, after loop interchange, also for the second.
    A[i, j]: in  DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j      # row-major: A[i][j]
    x1[i]:   inout DATA_TYPE = i -> i                # dense 1D, unit stride
    x2[i]:   inout DATA_TYPE = i -> i                # dense 1D, unit stride
    y1[j]:   in  DATA_TYPE = j -> j                  # dense 1D, unit stride
    y2[j]:   in  DATA_TYPE = j -> j                  # dense 1D, unit stride

parameters:
    N:   int        # problem size, N x N
    T_I: int        # tile size for i (rows), tuned for L2/L3 cache
    T_J: int        # tile size for j (cols), tuned for SIMD & cache
    V:   int        # SIMD width for vectorization over j or i

computation:
    # First matrix–vector product:
    #   x1[i] = x1[i] + sum_j A[i][j] * y1[j]
    K1:
        for i:
            x1[i] = x1[i] + sum(j, A[i, j] * y1[j])

    # Second matrix–vector product (using A^T):
    #   x2[i] = x2[i] + sum_j A[j][i] * y2[j]
    K2:
        for i:
            x2[i] = x2[i] + sum(j, A[j, i] * y2[j])

optimization:
    # ---------------------------------------------
    # Common data-layout and tiling strategy
    # ---------------------------------------------
    # A is already row-major with j as the unit-stride dimension:
    #   A[i, j] -> i * N + j
    # This makes accesses A[i, j] with j in the innermost loop contiguous.

    # ---------------------------------------------
    # Optimize K1: x1[i] += A[i, :] · y1[:]
    # ---------------------------------------------
    # Tile (block) both i and j so each tile of A and y1 fits in cache.
    block(i, I1, T_I)    # outer tile index I1 over rows
    block(j, J1, T_J)    # outer tile index J1 over cols

    # Bring tile loops outermost: iterate over tiles, then within-tile points.
    hoist(I1)
    hoist(J1)

    # Within each tile, we want j (the reduction index) to be the
    # innermost loop to exploit contiguous A[i, j] and y1[j] accesses.
    # The default nesting after block+hoist is:
    #   for I1:
    #     for J1:
    #       for i in tile I1:
    #         for j in tile J1:
    #           ...
    # which already has j innermost.

    # Vectorize the innermost j-loop to exploit SIMD on:
    #   - loads A[i, j...j+V-1]
    #   - loads y1[j...j+V-1]
    #   - updates of a vectorized accumulator for x1[i]
    vectorize(j, V)

    # Parallelize across tiles in the i-dimension: each i (row) is independent
    # in K1, so different threads can own disjoint i-ranges without races.
    parallelize(I1)

    # ---------------------------------------------
    # Optimize K2: x2[i] += A^T[i, :] · y2[:]
    # ---------------------------------------------
    # Original semantics:
    #   for i:
    #     for j:
    #       x2[i] += A[j, i] * y2[j]
    #
    # We first apply loop interchange to get better spatial locality in A:
    #   for j:
    #     for i:
    #       x2[i] += A[j, i] * y2[j]
    #
    # Now A[j, i] has j as the row index, and with row-major layout
    #   A[j, i] -> j * N + i
    # so the inner loop over i walks a contiguous row of A.
    interchange(i, j)  # applied to K2 only

    # Tile (block) both j and i for K2 as well.
    block(j, J2, T_J)  # tile over rows of A (index j)
    block(i, I2, T_I)  # tile over cols of A (index i)

    # Make tile loops outermost for K2.
    hoist(J2)
    hoist(I2)

    # In the interchanged form of K2:
    #   for J2:
    #     for I2:
    #       for j in tile J2:
    #         for i in tile I2:
    #           x2[i] += A[j, i] * y2[j]
    # The innermost loop walks i, which is contiguous in memory for
    #    A[j, i] and x2[i], so we vectorize in i.
    vectorize(i, V)

    # Parallelize over j-tiles J2:
    #   - Each j (and thus each J2 tile) has an independent contribution
    #     to x2[*] from y2[j], so splitting over J2 is safe.
    #   - The updates to x2[i] are associative and commutative in j, and
    #     can be implemented with per-thread partial sums for x2[*] and a
    #     final reduction, or with atomic adds if available.
    parallelize(J2)

    # ---------------------------------------------
    # Optional higher-level optimization (algorithmic fusion)
    # ---------------------------------------------
    # #fuse(K1, K2)  # custom directive (conceptual):
    # #  Iterate once over tiles of (i, j) and update both x1 and x2:
    # #    x1[i] += A[i, j] * y1[j]
    # #    x2[j] += A[i, j] * y2[i]
    # #
    # #  This reduces A loads by ~2× by reusing A[i, j] for both products.
    # #  When combined with tiling and vectorization as above, this further
    # #  improves cache reuse. Parallelization over tiles must then implement
    # #  x2 as a reduction over i (e.g., via per-thread x2_partial[j] and a
    # #  final reduction step) to avoid races.
```

domain:
    i: dim in [0, N)        # logical row index
    j: dim in [0, N)        # logical column index

data:
    # Dense N×N matrix A, with C semantics A[i][j]; row-major layout.
    # Address of A[i, j] is i * N + j.
    A[i, j]: in num_t = (i, j) -> i * N + j

    # Input vectors (initial values).
    x1_init[i]: in  num_t = i -> i
    x2_init[i]: in  num_t = i -> i
    y1[j]:      in  num_t = j -> j
    y2[j]:      in  num_t = j -> j

    # Output vectors (final values). In the C code these alias x1, x2 in-place,
    # but here we model them as distinct for clarity.
    x1[i]: out num_t = i -> i
    x2[i]: out num_t = i -> i

parameters:
    # Tuning parameters for scheduling (chosen based on cache size and SIMD width).
    TI: int   # tile size for i (e.g., 128 or 256)
    TJ: int   # tile size for j / reduction (e.g., 256 or 512)
    V:  int   # SIMD vector width along innermost dimension (e.g., 4 for double, 8 for float)

computation:
    # Kernel 1: x1[i] = x1[i] + sum_j A[i][j] * y1[j]
    # (Matrix–vector product using each row of A.)
    for i in [0, N):
        x1[i] = x1_init[i] + sum(j in [0, N), A[i, j] * y1[j])

    # Kernel 2: x2[i] = x2[i] + sum_j A[j][i] * y2[j]
    # (Transpose-matrix–vector product using each column of A.)
    for i in [0, N):
        x2[i] = x2_init[i] + sum(j in [0, N), A[j, i] * y2[j])

dependencies:
    # x1 and x2 computations are independent: they read only A, y1, y2,
    # and their own input vectors. No cross-dependence:
    #   ∀i: x1(i) does not depend on x2(*), and x2(i) does not depend on x1(*).
    # Therefore, the two kernels can be executed in any order, in parallel,
    # or fused into a single traversal over i without changing semantics.

optimization:
    # Overall strategy:
    #   - Keep A row‑major as in C: A[i, j] contiguous in j.
    #   - For kernel 1 (row-based M·v), iterate j innermost to get stride‑1
    #     accesses to A[i, j] and y1[j]; vectorize over j.
    #   - For kernel 2 (column-based Mᵀ·v), interchange loops so that we
    #     iterate over i innermost while holding j fixed, which gives
    #     stride‑1 accesses to A[j, i]; vectorize over i.
    #   - Tile i to expose parallelism and improve cache locality.
    #   - Keep extra memory usage to O(TI) scalars (well under +50%).

    # 1) Tile i to get coarse-grain parallelism and better cache reuse of rows/columns.
    #    i = I_tile * TI + i_inner
    block(i, I_tile, TI)
    parallelize(I_tile)      # distribute tiles of rows across cores (x1 and x2 can also run on different threads/tasks)

    # 2) Kernel 1 (x1 update): keep j as innermost loop over each row of A.
    #    This gives stride‑1 access to A[i, j] and y1[j].
    #
    #    Optional blocking of j (mainly for very large N) so that y1 and the
    #    current row slice of A stay in L1/L2:
    block(j, J1_tile, TJ)
    #    Within each J1_tile, iterate j innermost and use SIMD:
    vectorize(j, V)          # vectorize the reduction over contiguous j for A[i, j] * y1[j]

    # 3) Kernel 2 (x2 update): access A[j, i].
    #    With A row-major, A[j, i] is contiguous in i, not in j. To get stride‑1
    #    access we interchange the loops so i is innermost for this kernel.
    #
    #    We conceptually tile both i and j as for kernel 1:
    block(j, J2_tile, TJ)
    #    and then perform a loop interchange inside each tile:
    interchange(j, i)        # inside each {I_tile, J2_tile} tile: run J2_tile (j) outer, i inner
    vectorize(i, V)          # SIMD across contiguous i for A[j, i] * y2[j]

    # 4) Hoist invariant loads of y1[j] and y2[j].
    #    When j is outer and i is inner (kernel 2), y2[j] is loop-invariant
    #    with respect to i and should be loaded once per (j or J2_tile),
    #    then reused across all i in the tile.
    #    Similarly in kernel 1, y1[j] is invariant with respect to i.
    hoist(j)                 # conceptually: load y1[j]/y2[j] once per j (or j-block), not per i

    # 5) Optional fusion of the two kernels over i:
    #    for each tile I_tile and each i in that tile, compute both x1[i]
    #    and x2[i] in a single pass over j. This reuses y1[j] and y2[j] in cache
    #    and can improve TLB/cache behavior without extra storage:
    #
    #    for I_tile:
    #      for i in tile:
    #        acc1 = x1_init[i]
    #        acc2 = x2_init[i]
    #        for j:
    #          acc1 += A[i, j] * y1[j]
    #          acc2 += A[j, i] * y2[j]
    #        x1[i] = acc1
    #        x2[i] = acc2
    #
    #    # This is an algorithmically equivalent loop fusion and respects
    #    # the original semantics, while retaining the tiling/parallelization
    #    # directives above (parallel over I_tile, vectorized inner loops).
    #
    #    (No new directive keyword added; this fusion is a legal reordering
    #     implied by the absence of dependencies between the two kernels.)

```text
domain:
    # N is the global problem size (from defines.hpp)
    i: dim in [0, N)
    j: dim in [0, N)

data:
    # Matrix A and vectors x1, x2, y1, y2.
    #
    # Use a row‑major layout for A so that A[i, j] (row i, column j)
    # is stored contiguously in j; this gives good locality for the
    # first matvec and, after loop interchange, also for the second.
    A[i, j]: in  DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j     # row-major
    x1[i]:   inout DATA_TYPE = (i) -> i             # contiguous 1D
    x2[i]:   inout DATA_TYPE = (i) -> i             # contiguous 1D
    y1[j]:   in  DATA_TYPE = (j) -> j               # contiguous 1D
    y2[j]:   in  DATA_TYPE = (j) -> j               # contiguous 1D

parameters:
    # Tuning parameters (compile-time / launch-time constants).
    TI: int  # tile size in i, e.g. 64 (rows of A)
    TJ: int  # tile size in j, e.g. 64 (columns of A)
    V:  int  # SIMD vector width along the inner dimension, e.g. 8 for AVX2 doubles
    U:  int  # small unroll factor for the innermost loop, e.g. 2 or 4

computation:
    # First kernel:
    #   for (i) for (j) x1[i] += A[i][j] * y1[j];
    #
    # Expressed as a reduction over j:
    X1_UPDATE:
        for i in [0, N):
            x1[i] = x1[i] + sum(j in [0, N), A[i, j] * y1[j])

    # Second kernel:
    #   for (i) for (j) x2[i] += A[j][i] * y2[j];
    #
    # This is the matvec with A^T. We keep the same mathematical form
    # (sum over j of A[j, i] * y2[j]) but will access A with good
    # spatial locality via loop interchange in the optimization section.
    X2_UPDATE:
        for i in [0, N):
            x2[i] = x2[i] + sum(j in [0, N), A[j, i] * y2[j])

dependencies:
    # The x1 and x2 updates are independent and can be executed in any order.
    # There are no cross-dependencies between X1_UPDATE and X2_UPDATE.
    # (Both read A, y1, y2 but write disjoint vectors x1 and x2.)
    # Hence:
    #   X1_UPDATE(i) and X2_UPDATE(k) are independent for all i, k.

optimization:
    # -------------------------
    # Optimizations for X1_UPDATE
    # -------------------------
    # X1_UPDATE is a standard dense matrix–vector product with row-major
    # A and inner loop over j. We block, parallelize, and vectorize
    # over contiguous j for good cache and SIMD efficiency.

    # Tile i (rows) and j (columns) so each A tile of size TI×TJ fits
    # comfortably in cache (rough guideline: TI * TJ * sizeof(DATA_TYPE)
    # <= last-level-cache / #threads).
    block(i, I1, TI)        # i = I1 * TI + ii
    block(j, J1, TJ)        # j = J1 * TJ + jj

    # Parallelize over outer i-tiles: each tile updates a disjoint
    # subset of x1, so there are no write conflicts.
    parallelize(I1)         # multi-core over coarse-grain row tiles

    # Within each tile, keep row-major traversal:
    #   for I1     (parallel)
    #     for J1
    #       for ii in [0, TI)
    #         for jj in [0, TJ)
    #           x1[I1*TI+ii] += A[I1*TI+ii, J1*TJ+jj] * y1[J1*TJ+jj]
    #
    # Vectorize jj, which maps to contiguous columns j of A and y1.
    vectorize(j, V)         # SIMD over jj (inner columns within a row)
    unroll(j, U)            # small unroll on jj to reduce loop overhead

    # Optional: slight unroll on the inner ii loop to expose more ILP.
    # unroll(i, U)          # inside each (I1, J1) tile, if profitable

    # -------------------------
    # Optimizations for X2_UPDATE
    # -------------------------
    # X2_UPDATE is logically:
    #   x2[i] += sum_j A[j, i] * y2[j]
    #
    # With row-major A, A[j, i] is stored in row j, column i.
    # To get good locality, we interchange i and j in the *kernel*
    # (but not in the mathematical definition):
    #
    #   for j in [0, N):
    #     for i in [0, N):
    #       x2[i] += A[j, i] * y2[j]
    #
    # This traverses each row j of A contiguously in i.

    interchange(i, j) in X2_UPDATE
    # After interchange, j is outer, i is inner for X2_UPDATE.

    # Block j and i similarly, but note that we will not parallelize
    # across j-tiles without privatization of x2 (to avoid races),
    # so we focus on SIMD and cache-friendly blocking here.

    block(j, J2, TJ)        # j = J2 * TJ + jj
    block(i, I2, TI)        # i = I2 * TI + ii

    # Vectorize i (inner dimension) to exploit contiguous access to A[j, i]
    # in row-major storage. Using the same V as above simplifies tuning.
    vectorize(i, V)         # SIMD over ii within a row of A
    unroll(i, U)            # small unroll on ii

    # Parallelization strategy:
    #   - We parallelize the outer i-tiles of X1_UPDATE (above), which
    #     typically dominates runtime.
    #   - X2_UPDATE uses efficient row-major traversal and SIMD but is
    #     kept sequential in j to avoid write contention on x2.
    #
    # If additional parallelism is desired and extra memory N * T
    # (T = #threads) is acceptable (< 50% of A’s N^2 storage for N >= 64),
    # we can privatize x2 and parallelize J2:
    #
    #   #parallelize_with_privatization(J2, x2)
    #
    # where:
    #   #parallelize_with_privatization(DIM, ARRAY)
    #   #  means: create a private copy ARRAY_private[DIM, i] per parallel
    #   #  worker, accumulate into it in parallel over DIM, and at the end
    #   #  reduce (sum) all private copies into the global ARRAY. This
    #   #  removes write conflicts while adding only O(N * #threads) extra
    #   #  storage, which is at most a small fraction of the N^2 matrix.
```

domain:
    i: dim in [0, N)
    j: dim in [0, N)

data:
    # 2D matrix, logical A[i][j] in the original C code.
    # Stored row-major so j is the unit‑stride (innermost) dimension.
    A[i, j]: in DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j  # row-major

    # 1D vectors, contiguous.
    x1[i]: inout DATA_TYPE = i
    x2[i]: inout DATA_TYPE = i
    y1[j]: in DATA_TYPE = j
    y2[j]: in DATA_TYPE = j

parameters:
    # Tunable tile sizes for cache blocking.
    I_BLOCK: int  # e.g., 64 or 128, chosen to balance cache and parallelism
    J_BLOCK: int  # e.g., 256 or 512

    # Tunable SIMD width; should match hardware vector width in elements.
    VEC_WIDTH: int  # e.g., 8 for AVX2 float, 4 for AVX2 double

computation:
    # First kernel:
    #   for (i) for (j) x1[i] += A[i][j] * y1[j];
    X1:
        for i in [0, N):
            x1[i] = x1[i] + sum(j1 in [0, N), A[i, j1] * y1[j1])

    # Second kernel:
    #   for (i) for (j) x2[i] += A[j][i] * y2[j];
    X2:
        for i in [0, N):
            x2[i] = x2[i] + sum(j2 in [0, N), A[j2, i] * y2[j2])

dependencies:
    # The two kernels are independent: x1 and x2 do not interact.
    # Either execution order is legal, and they may run concurrently.
    # (No explicit dependency needed.)
    # X1(i)  ->  X1(i, j1) reduction  # implied by the reduction itself
    # X2(i)  ->  X2(i, j2) reduction  # implied by the reduction itself

optimization:
    #--------------------------
    # Shared high-level strategy
    #--------------------------
    # – Keep A row-major and exploit its unit‑stride dimension in both kernels
    #   via suitable loop orders (no full transpose, so no large extra memory).
    # – Tile the i and j dimensions for cache locality.
    # – Parallelize across tiles of i (outermost work-sharing).
    # – Vectorize across the unit‑stride dimension inside each tile.
    # – Use separate schedules for X1 and X2 to match their access patterns.

    #--------------------------
    # Optimized schedule for X1
    # x1[i] += sum_j A[i,j] * y1[j]
    # Access pattern: A[i,*] (row), j is unit‑stride; x1[i] reused across j.
    #--------------------------
    X1:
        # Block rows and columns for better cache locality.
        # Outer tile index: I1; original i becomes the inner index within the tile.
        block(i, I1, I_BLOCK)
        # j1 is the reduction iterator; tile it as well so each tile works on
        # a contiguous slice of each row of A and y1.
        block(j1, J1, J_BLOCK)

        # Hoist the row-tile loop (I1) to the outermost level so that:
        #   for I1 (row tiles) in parallel:
        #     for i within tile:
        #       for J1 (column tiles):
        #         for j1 within tile:
        #           accumulate into x1[i]
        hoist(I1)

        # Parallelize over row tiles: each tile of rows is independent
        # (each i has its own x1[i] and reduction over j1).
        parallelize(I1)

        # Vectorize along the innermost unit‑stride dimension j1, to
        # efficiently load A[i, j1] and y1[j1] contiguously.
        vectorize(j1, VEC_WIDTH)

        # Optionally unroll small inner j1 or i loops within a tile to
        # reduce loop overhead and expose ILP.
        #unroll(j1, 4)

        # The loop order for the reduction in X1 is:
        #   for I1 (parallel)
        #     for i in tile
        #       for J1
        #         for j1 in tile (vectorized)

    #--------------------------
    # Optimized schedule for X2
    # x2[i] += sum_j A[j,i] * y2[j]
    # Default i-outer, j-inner order leads to strided access in A.
    # We interchange loops to make A[j,i] unit‑stride and x2[i] contiguous.
    #--------------------------
    X2:
        # Interchange i and j2 in the conceptual nested loops for this kernel:
        #   original: for i: for j2: x2[i] += A[j2,i] * y2[j2];
        #   optimized: for j2: for i: x2[i] += A[j2,i] * y2[j2];
        #
        # With A row-major (A[row, col] -> row = j2, col = i):
        #   – Inner loop over i walks A[j2, i] contiguously.
        #   – x2[i] is also updated contiguously.
        interchange(i, j2)

        # Now tile the (j2, i) space similarly to X1, but with j2 as outer tile
        # dimension and i as inner (contiguous) dimension.
        block(j2, J2, J_BLOCK)
        block(i, I2, I_BLOCK)

        # Hoist the j2-tile loop to the outermost level:
        #   for J2 (tiles over j2) in parallel:
        #     for j2 in tile:
        #       for I2 (tiles over i):
        #         for i in tile:
        #           accumulate into x2[i]
        hoist(J2)

        # Parallelize over tiles of j2: each j2 tile contributes independently
        # to all x2[i]; the accumulation across j2 tiles is associative/commutative,
        # so parallel reduction across tiles is legal (modulo FP roundoff).
        parallelize(J2)

        # Vectorize across i, which is the unit‑stride dimension for both
        # A[j2, i] and x2[i].
        vectorize(i, VEC_WIDTH)

        # Optionally unroll a small inner loop for more ILP.
        #unroll(i, 4)

    #--------------------------

    #   # This reuses tiles of A and y-vectors across both kernels without
    #   # increasing asymptotic memory usage (no full A transpose is stored).
